This practice material is designed to help you make and justify sampling decisions. Each question presents a short research situation. Enter or select an answer before opening the explanation, then compare the suggested reasoning with your own. The explanations often discuss why an alternative design would answer a *different* question, or why an apparently sensible design would not support the intended conclusion.

The exercises draw on the ideas developed particularly in [Chapter 1](01-inquiry.qmd), [Chapter 2](02-system-understanding.qmd), [Chapter 5](05-sampling-replication.qmd), [Chapter 6](06-space.qmd), [Chapter 7](07-time.qmd), [Chapter 8](08-mobile-organisms.qmd), [Chapter 9](09-experiments.qmd), and Chapters [10](10-quantitative-socioenvironmental.qmd)–[12](12-socioenvironmental-explanations.qmd). You do not need to read them again before starting; use the links when an explanation reveals something worth revisiting.

The final design challenge uses the assignment's **three-year** period and **720 person-hour** fieldwork allowance. Its landscape and cost estimates are invented for practice; they do not describe the particular restoration landscape in your assignment.

<div class="practice-legend" role="note"><strong>How to use this page:</strong> Choose or type an answer. When the <em>Show explained answer</em> button becomes available, select it to see the reasoning. Your answer stays visible. Multiple-choice and matching questions indicate whether your choices match the suggested answers. You can change your response and try again.</div>

## A. From the research question to the sampling design

A sampling strategy only makes sense in relation to the population, relationship or process you want to study. These exercises start with that decision.


::: {.practice-exercise #practice-01 data-mode="matching"}

<span class="practice-number">Exercise 1</span>

**One landscape, four research questions**

A restored landscape contains planted stands, naturally regenerating areas, streams and walking paths. Each question below calls for a different sampling strategy. Match the question to the design that would provide the most useful starting point.

**Your task.** Choose the most informative design for each question.

<div class="practice-response" data-mode="matching">
<div class="practice-matches"><p class="practice-label">Choose one design or interpretation for each statement.</p>
<label class="practice-match"><span class="practice-match-statement">Estimate mean stand basal area per hectare across all wooded land in the landscape.</span><select aria-label="Match for item 1 in exercise 01" data-answer="D"><option value="">Choose…</option>
<option value="A">A. Select several separate stands in each restoration category, with plots within stands and attention to initial conditions.</option>
<option value="B">B. Sample at several planned distances from the remnant forest, in more than one part of the landscape.</option>
<option value="C">C. Recruit path users and people who do not use the path, across relevant times and groups.</option>
<option value="D">D. Select locations across the whole defined wooded area using a probability-based sampling frame.</option>
</select></label>
<label class="practice-match"><span class="practice-match-statement">Compare seedling recruitment between planted and naturally regenerating stands.</span><select aria-label="Match for item 2 in exercise 01" data-answer="A"><option value="">Choose…</option>
<option value="A">A. Select several separate stands in each restoration category, with plots within stands and attention to initial conditions.</option>
<option value="B">B. Sample at several planned distances from the remnant forest, in more than one part of the landscape.</option>
<option value="C">C. Recruit path users and people who do not use the path, across relevant times and groups.</option>
<option value="D">D. Select locations across the whole defined wooded area using a probability-based sampling frame.</option>
</select></label>
<label class="practice-match"><span class="practice-match-statement">Investigate how seedling establishment varies with distance from a remnant forest.</span><select aria-label="Match for item 3 in exercise 01" data-answer="B"><option value="">Choose…</option>
<option value="A">A. Select several separate stands in each restoration category, with plots within stands and attention to initial conditions.</option>
<option value="B">B. Sample at several planned distances from the remnant forest, in more than one part of the landscape.</option>
<option value="C">C. Recruit path users and people who do not use the path, across relevant times and groups.</option>
<option value="D">D. Select locations across the whole defined wooded area using a probability-based sampling frame.</option>
</select></label>
<label class="practice-match"><span class="practice-match-statement">Understand why some residents avoid a particular walking path.</span><select aria-label="Match for item 4 in exercise 01" data-answer="C"><option value="">Choose…</option>
<option value="A">A. Select several separate stands in each restoration category, with plots within stands and attention to initial conditions.</option>
<option value="B">B. Sample at several planned distances from the remnant forest, in more than one part of the landscape.</option>
<option value="C">C. Recruit path users and people who do not use the path, across relevant times and groups.</option>
<option value="D">D. Select locations across the whole defined wooded area using a probability-based sampling frame.</option>
</select></label>
</div>
</div>
<div class="practice-actions"><button type="button" class="practice-reveal" disabled aria-controls="practice-solution-01" aria-expanded="false">Show explained answer</button><span class="practice-status" aria-live="polite"></span></div>

::: {.practice-solution #practice-solution-01 hidden="hidden"}

**Suggested answer and reasoning**

1. **Begin with what each question asks you to describe or compare.** An *average across the wooded landscape* is a different objective from *comparing planted and naturally regenerating stands*. The first concerns all eligible wooded land; the second requires good representation of both management categories.
2. **Landscape mean — D.** Define what counts as wooded land, and choose locations from that whole area using a probability-based procedure. Every eligible part should have a known chance of selection. If you deliberately sample some habitats more intensively, an overall mean may need to take the areas or selection probabilities into account.
3. **Restoration comparison — A.** Include several separate stands under each approach, then use plots within those stands. Ten plots in one planted stand cannot replace observations from several planted stands: otherwise management is mixed up with all the other characteristics of that particular stand.
4. **Distance from mature forest — B.** Cover short, intermediate and long distances, ideally in several landscape sectors. A sample confined to nearby locations would tell you little about what happens farther away.
5. **Path avoidance — C.** Speak to people who use the path **and** people who do not. Interviewing only users cannot tell you why others stay away. Sampling at different times may also reveal different experiences.

The lesson is not to memorise four named sampling techniques. First ask *which variation or comparison is needed to answer this question?* Then choose where and whom to sample.

:::

:::


::: {.practice-exercise #practice-02 data-mode="single"}

<span class="practice-number">Exercise 2</span>

**Is simple random sampling enough?**

A project asks whether measured soil infiltration differs among planted woodland, naturally regenerating woodland and unrestored grassland. The three land covers occupy unequal areas. The team can establish 24 infiltration plots.

**Your task.** Which sampling proposal provides the clearest starting point for this question?

<div class="practice-response" data-mode="single">
<fieldset class="practice-choices" data-correct="B"><legend>Select the best answer</legend>
<label class="practice-choice"><input type="radio" name="practice-group-02" value="A"><span><b>A.</b> Draw 24 random locations across the whole landscape without distinguishing land cover.</span></label>
<label class="practice-choice"><input type="radio" name="practice-group-02" value="B"><span><b>B.</b> Define the three categories, include several separate sites in each, and select plots within those sites.</span></label>
<label class="practice-choice"><input type="radio" name="practice-group-02" value="C"><span><b>C.</b> Put all 24 plots close to the main access road to reduce field time.</span></label>
</fieldset>
</div>
<div class="practice-actions"><button type="button" class="practice-reveal" disabled aria-controls="practice-solution-02" aria-expanded="false">Show explained answer</button><span class="practice-status" aria-live="polite"></span></div>

::: {.practice-solution #practice-solution-02 hidden="hidden"}

**Suggested answer and reasoning**

1. **Identify the comparison.** The question concerns infiltration in *three land-cover categories*. You therefore need enough information from each category to describe and compare them.
2. **See why A is weak here.** If most of the landscape is grassland, a completely random sample of 24 points may place most plots in grassland and only a few in the two woodland categories. You might estimate a landscape-wide average, but you would have little basis for comparing all three categories.
3. **Choose B.** Delineate the three categories, include several separately located sites in each, and select plots within those sites. You could select sites or plots randomly *within* the categories. The important decision—ensuring coverage of every category—comes **before** the random draw.
4. **Notice the difference between sites and plots.** Several plots in one planted stand tell you about that stand. To learn about planted woodland more generally, sample several planted stands. The same applies to the other land covers.
5. **Keep the conclusion appropriate.** The study can describe how infiltration differs among the sampled categories. But different land covers may also occur on different soils or slopes. A difference would not automatically show that restoration *caused* the infiltration difference.

Option C is convenient, but convenient roadside locations may not represent the environments the question is about. Think about the comparison first, and accessibility second.

:::

:::


::: {.practice-exercise #practice-03 data-mode="single"}

<span class="practice-number">Exercise 3</span>

**What is the target population?**

A field team wants to estimate mean soil carbon stock per hectare in the upper metre of sediment across *all mangrove habitat* on an island. They collect 40 cores of that depth at eight accessible locations.

**Your task.** Which statement best identifies the target population?

<div class="practice-response" data-mode="single">
<fieldset class="practice-choices" data-correct="C"><legend>Select the best answer</legend>
<label class="practice-choice"><input type="radio" name="practice-group-03" value="A"><span><b>A.</b> The 40 cores collected.</span></label>
<label class="practice-choice"><input type="radio" name="practice-group-03" value="B"><span><b>B.</b> The eight sampled locations.</span></label>
<label class="practice-choice"><input type="radio" name="practice-group-03" value="C"><span><b>C.</b> The mangrove sediment area of the island about which the study wants to draw conclusions.</span></label>
<label class="practice-choice"><input type="radio" name="practice-group-03" value="D"><span><b>D.</b> All coastal wetlands worldwide.</span></label>
</fieldset>
</div>
<div class="practice-actions"><button type="button" class="practice-reveal" disabled aria-controls="practice-solution-03" aria-expanded="false">Show explained answer</button><span class="practice-status" aria-live="polite"></span></div>

::: {.practice-solution #practice-solution-03 hidden="hidden"}

**Suggested answer and reasoning**

1. **Ask which area the conclusion is meant to describe.** The team wants a mean stock for the upper metre of sediment across the island's *entire mangrove habitat*. That is the target area: **C**.
2. **Distinguish the target from the sample.** The eight sampled locations and 40 cores are the places and soil volumes actually observed. They are **not** the whole population about which the team wants to make a claim. Option D is far too broad; the team is not studying wetlands worldwide.
3. **Why does the distinction affect the design?** Suppose the eight locations are all beside accessible boardwalks. If inaccessible mangroves have different sediment conditions, averaging these cores may not describe the whole island. More cores beside the same boardwalk do not fix that coverage problem.
4. **Recognise the sampling levels.** Several cores at one location improve the estimate of that location's sediment stock. More locations distributed across the island help describe differences *among locations*. Both can be useful, but they answer different needs.
5. **Keep depth consistent.** The target is the upper metre, so the soil measurements and stock calculations must refer to that defined layer. Carbon concentration alone is not a stock; bulk density and sampled depth are also needed.

Before designing a sample, finish this sentence: *I want my estimate to represent ______.* That blank identifies the target population or area.

:::

:::


::: {.practice-exercise #practice-04 data-mode="single"}

<span class="practice-number">Exercise 4</span>

**Sampling along a gradient**

A mangrove researcher proposes that seedling survival decreases as the duration of flooding increases. Most accessible sites experience shorter flooding, while the longest-flooded sites are difficult to reach. Seedlings would be marked and revisited to record survival.

**Your task.** What would be the strongest design choice for investigating the proposed relationship?

<div class="practice-response" data-mode="single">
<fieldset class="practice-choices" data-correct="B"><legend>Select the best answer</legend>
<label class="practice-choice"><input type="radio" name="practice-group-04" value="A"><span><b>A.</b> Select sites only where access is easiest and add more seedlings per site.</span></label>
<label class="practice-choice"><input type="radio" name="practice-group-04" value="B"><span><b>B.</b> Select sites spanning short, intermediate and long hydroperiods, with replicated locations, and monitor seedlings there.</span></label>
<label class="practice-choice"><input type="radio" name="practice-group-04" value="C"><span><b>C.</b> Sample many seedlings at one intermediate site and use it to represent the entire gradient.</span></label>
</fieldset>
</div>
<div class="practice-actions"><button type="button" class="practice-reveal" disabled aria-controls="practice-solution-04" aria-expanded="false">Show explained answer</button><span class="practice-status" aria-live="polite"></span></div>

::: {.practice-solution #practice-solution-04 hidden="hidden"}

**Suggested answer and reasoning**

1. **Translate the question into a comparison.** The hypothesis is about survival under *different flooding durations*. A useful design needs seedlings exposed to short, intermediate and long flooding.
2. **Choose B.** Sampling only easy-to-reach, briefly flooded sites (**A**) leaves out the most important part of the gradient. Sampling many seedlings at one site (**C**) gives detailed information about that site, not about the range of flooding conditions.
3. **Replicate locations, not only seedlings.** If one long-flooded site has poor survival, this could be caused by salinity, sediment conditions or another feature of that particular site. Several locations at each part of the hydroperiod gradient give a stronger comparison.
4. **Measure the conditions and response appropriately.** Record flooding duration at or near the seedling locations, preferably over representative periods. Mark seedlings and revisit them to find out which survive. If different species occupy different parts of the gradient, compare like with like or explicitly account for species.
5. **Think about what you can conclude.** You can investigate whether survival and flooding duration are associated. Because salinity, elevation and soil properties may also change with flooding, the design must consider these alternative explanations before attributing survival differences to flooding alone.

A targeted gradient design is appropriate here because it ensures that the environmental variation central to the question is actually sampled.

:::

:::


::: {.practice-exercise #practice-05 data-mode="text"}

<span class="practice-number">Exercise 5</span>

**What would you draw on the map?**

You propose selecting 12 locations in a restoration landscape to investigate erosion on hillslopes. The map includes gentle and steep slopes, fenced areas and stream margins. Simply choosing 12 random points anywhere on the map could miss important differences among hillslopes.

**Your task.** Explain what you would mark on the map, which locations would qualify for sampling, and how you would choose the 12 sites. You do not need to specify all 12 final coordinates.

<div class="practice-response" data-mode="text">
<label class="practice-label" for="practice-input-05">Your answer</label>
<textarea id="practice-input-05" class="practice-text" rows="3" placeholder="Write a brief answer. Explain your sampling decision and why it fits the question."></textarea>
</div>
<div class="practice-actions"><button type="button" class="practice-reveal" disabled aria-controls="practice-solution-05" aria-expanded="false">Show explained answer</button><span class="practice-status" aria-live="polite"></span></div>

::: {.practice-solution #practice-solution-05 hidden="hidden"}

**Suggested answer and reasoning**

1. **First identify the area relevant to the question.** The question is about erosion *on hillslopes*. Mark the hillslopes on the map and decide, with a reason, whether stream channels or flat ground belong in the sampling frame. Do not choose random points from the whole landscape before making that decision.
2. **Look for variation likely to affect erosion.** Steep and gentle slopes, land cover, soil type and management history may differ. If the question is about these differences, the sample must represent them. One option is to divide hillslopes into slope or land-cover categories (strata).
3. **State how you would choose 12 sites.** For example, allocate a number of sites to each slope class, then draw locations randomly *within* each defined class. You can show the classes or candidate areas on the map and explain the selection procedure; the assignment need not specify every final GPS coordinate.
4. **Deal with access rather than silently ignoring it.** A fence may require permission; a very steep location may be difficult or unsafe. If important locations cannot be sampled, explain which conditions are missing and how that limits the proposed conclusion.
5. **Explain what is replicated.** Twelve plots on one hillside provide many observations of that hillside. If the aim is to understand erosion across the landscape, distribute sites among separate hillslopes as well.

Random selection can be part of a good design, but it cannot determine *what* should be sampled. The question and the relevant environmental variation must do that.

:::

:::


::: {.practice-exercise #practice-06 data-mode="matching"}

<span class="practice-number">Exercise 6</span>

**Solid and dashed arrows**

A team is investigating how vegetation might influence water movement in a restored catchment. Its model includes these proposed links: canopy openness affects light below the trees; vegetation development may change roots, litter and soil structure, which can affect infiltration; infiltration may, in turn, influence runoff. The team measures canopy openness and understory light at the same plots, records soil bulk density, and measures runoff at the catchment outlet. It does **not** measure roots, litter or infiltration.

Here, a **solid arrow** means the proposed study can examine the particular link fairly directly with relevant observations and comparisons. A **dashed arrow** means that interpretation of the link depends substantially on unmeasured processes or assumptions. Neither kind of arrow, by itself, establishes causation.

**Your task.** Decide which links are examined directly and which remain indirect **in this study**. After making your choices, consider this: would measuring infiltration make the canopy–infiltration link a direct causal relationship?

<div class="practice-response" data-mode="matching">
<div class="practice-matches"><p class="practice-label">Choose one design or interpretation for each statement.</p>
<label class="practice-match"><span class="practice-match-statement">Canopy openness → understory light, examined with paired measurements across plots under comparable light conditions.</span><select aria-label="Match for item 1 in exercise 06" data-answer="S"><option value="">Choose…</option>
<option value="S">S. Solid: the study examines the specific proposed link fairly directly.</option>
<option value="D">D. Dashed: the link is inferred mainly through other observations and assumptions.</option>
</select></label>
<label class="practice-match"><span class="practice-match-statement">Canopy openness → infiltration, interpreted from canopy observations and bulk density, without measuring roots, litter or infiltration.</span><select aria-label="Match for item 2 in exercise 06" data-answer="D"><option value="">Choose…</option>
<option value="S">S. Solid: the study examines the specific proposed link fairly directly.</option>
<option value="D">D. Dashed: the link is inferred mainly through other observations and assumptions.</option>
</select></label>
<label class="practice-match"><span class="practice-match-statement">Soil infiltration → catchment runoff, inferred from outlet runoff records and existing knowledge, without measuring infiltration or the intervening catchment processes.</span><select aria-label="Match for item 3 in exercise 06" data-answer="D"><option value="">Choose…</option>
<option value="S">S. Solid: the study examines the specific proposed link fairly directly.</option>
<option value="D">D. Dashed: the link is inferred mainly through other observations and assumptions.</option>
</select></label>
</div>
</div>
<div class="practice-actions"><button type="button" class="practice-reveal" disabled aria-controls="practice-solution-06" aria-expanded="false">Show explained answer</button><span class="practice-status" aria-live="polite"></span></div>

::: {.practice-solution #practice-solution-06 hidden="hidden"}

**Suggested answer and reasoning**

1. **Start with the first arrow: canopy openness → understory light.** The canopy controls how much of the sky and incoming light is obstructed above a point. The team measures canopy openness and light at matching locations, under comparable conditions. These observations address this link fairly directly, so **solid** is appropriate. Other influences on light, such as time of day and weather, still need attention.
2. **Now consider canopy openness → infiltration.** This is **dashed**. Canopy openness is a description of the vegetation *above the soil*. Water entering the soil depends on the soil's structure, pores and current moisture, among other things. Vegetation can influence those conditions through **roots, litter, organisms living in the soil and previous land use**. Canopy openness might be associated with some of those processes, but it does not measure them.
3. **What does soil bulk density add?** Bulk density tells us how much dry soil mass occupies a given volume. It can provide clues about compaction or pore space, but it is **not a measurement of infiltration**. Two soils with similar bulk density may allow water to enter at different rates because their pore structure, moisture or surface condition differs. The second arrow therefore remains dashed.
4. **Consider infiltration → catchment runoff.** This is also **dashed** in the proposed study. Runoff at a stream outlet collects water from many locations and processes. Rainfall, soil saturation, surface drainage, storage and channel flow all affect that total. Without suitable measurements and comparisons, an outlet record does not tell us how much runoff changed because of infiltration at the sampled plots.
5. **Would an infiltration measurement solve everything? No.** Measuring infiltration beside canopy observations would tell us whether *those measured quantities vary together*. It would not identify which roots, litter or soil processes connect them, or show that canopy openness itself caused the change. The canopy–infiltration *causal pathway* would still be indirect. To examine the mechanism more closely, we could measure relevant root or litter properties, soil structure and infiltration under informative contrasts.
6. **Remember what the arrow means.** A solid arrow does not announce that a causal effect has been proved. It means the study is designed to examine that particular relationship reasonably directly. A dashed arrow identifies a part of the proposed explanation that depends on additional reasoning and unmeasured links.

The answer is **solid, dashed, dashed**. Do not decide solely by whether you measured the variable at the beginning or end of an arrow. Ask what process the arrow represents, and whether your observations actually examine that process.

:::

:::


## B. Sampling across space and time

Good sampling requires choices about where observations are made, how many independent units are represented, and how effort is distributed through time.


::: {.practice-exercise #practice-07 data-mode="single"}

<span class="practice-number">Exercise 7</span>

**Plots versus independent restoration sites**

A student compares one planted forest with one naturally regenerating forest. Each contains 20 vegetation plots, and the student proposes a statistical comparison using 20 independent replicates per treatment.

**Your task.** What is the most consequential problem?

<div class="practice-response" data-mode="single">
<fieldset class="practice-choices" data-correct="B"><legend>Select the best answer</legend>
<label class="practice-choice"><input type="radio" name="practice-group-07" value="A"><span><b>A.</b> There are too few trees in each plot.</span></label>
<label class="practice-choice"><input type="radio" name="practice-group-07" value="B"><span><b>B.</b> There is only one forest of each treatment; plots cannot replicate the treatment comparison.</span></label>
<label class="practice-choice"><input type="radio" name="practice-group-07" value="C"><span><b>C.</b> The student should measure 40 plots in each forest.</span></label>
<label class="practice-choice"><input type="radio" name="practice-group-07" value="D"><span><b>D.</b> Repeated measurements would make all 40 plots independent.</span></label>
</fieldset>
</div>
<div class="practice-actions"><button type="button" class="practice-reveal" disabled aria-controls="practice-solution-07" aria-expanded="false">Show explained answer</button><span class="practice-status" aria-live="polite"></span></div>

::: {.practice-solution #practice-solution-07 hidden="hidden"}

**Suggested answer and reasoning**

1. **Find where the two approaches differ.** The planted approach was applied to one forest and natural regeneration to another. That makes **the forests** the units of the management comparison. There is one forest per approach.
2. **What are the 20 plots doing?** They describe variation *within* each forest. A forest with a mix of wetter and drier plots will give different values across plots, and having many plots helps estimate the forest's average. But every plot in a given forest shares that forest's management history and many other conditions.
3. **Why is B correct?** If the planted forest has more seedlings, that difference might reflect planting. It might also reflect soil, nearby seed sources, past farming or other differences between those two forests. With only one forest under each approach, the study cannot distinguish the approaches from those site differences.
4. **Improve the design at the right level.** Include several separate planted forests and several separate naturally regenerating forests. Use plots *within* them. Consider whether management was assigned or selected and whether initial conditions are comparable.
5. **Why the other options do not fix it.** More trees or plots inside the same two forests can improve their local estimates. Additional censuses track change through time. None of these creates new, independent forests under each approach.

This is a form of **pseudoreplication**: treating within-forest plots as though each were an independent replicate of the forest-level management treatment.

:::

:::


::: {.practice-exercise #practice-08 data-mode="fill"}

<span class="practice-number">Exercise 8</span>

**Where would you spend the same effort?**

You have enough field time for 48 vegetation plots to compare two restoration approaches across multiple independently located sites. Both designs use the same total number of plots: **Design X** samples two sites per approach, with 12 plots in each site. **Design Y** samples six sites per approach, with four plots in each site.

**Your task.** Fill in the site counts and name the design you would generally favour for a comparison intended to extend across restoration sites.

<div class="practice-response" data-mode="fill">
<div class="practice-fill">
<label class="practice-fill-row" for="practice-fill-08-0"><span>Independent sites per approach in Design X</span><input id="practice-fill-08-0" type="text" data-answer="2" placeholder="Enter answer" autocomplete="off"></label>
<label class="practice-fill-row" for="practice-fill-08-1"><span>Independent sites per approach in Design Y</span><input id="practice-fill-08-1" type="text" data-answer="6" placeholder="Enter answer" autocomplete="off"></label>
<label class="practice-fill-row" for="practice-fill-08-2"><span>Preferred design (X or Y)</span><input id="practice-fill-08-2" type="text" data-answer="Y" placeholder="Enter answer" autocomplete="off"></label>
</div>
</div>
<div class="practice-actions"><button type="button" class="practice-reveal" disabled aria-controls="practice-solution-08" aria-expanded="false">Show explained answer</button><span class="practice-status" aria-live="polite"></span></div>

::: {.practice-solution #practice-solution-08 hidden="hidden"}

**Suggested answer and reasoning**

1. **Count the independent sites, not only the plots.** Design X samples **two sites per approach**. Design Y samples **six sites per approach**. Both have 24 plots per approach and 48 plots in total.
2. **Identify what the question needs.** The aim is to compare restoration approaches *across sites*. Differences among separate sites are therefore an important part of the variation the study must represent.
3. **Why favour Y?** With six sites per approach, Y provides information about how results vary among sites. X can measure each of its four sites in more detail, but cannot describe the broader variation among restoration sites as well.
4. **What is lost by choosing Y?** Each site has only four plots rather than twelve. If conditions within a site are very heterogeneous, four plots may estimate its mean less precisely. A good design balances the need for site-level replication with adequate measurements inside sites.
5. **Check practical and causal limits.** Travelling to twelve sites might take more time than visiting four. Also, if one approach occurs only on steep slopes and the other on gentle slopes, adding sites alone will not distinguish management from slope. Site selection must consider such differences.

**Y** is the better starting point *for the question given*, assuming the twelve sites are meaningfully separate and the within-site plots adequately describe them. The best design can be different if the question instead concerns variation within one specific forest.

:::

:::


::: {.practice-exercise #practice-09 data-mode="single"}

<span class="practice-number">Exercise 9</span>

**Twelve plots along one stream**

To investigate whether streamside vegetation is related to bank erosion across a watershed, a researcher measures twelve plots spaced ten metres apart along one stream. Another researcher proposes three plots on each of four streams.

**Your task.** What is the main advantage of the second design for this watershed-level question?

<div class="practice-response" data-mode="single">
<fieldset class="practice-choices" data-correct="B"><legend>Select the best answer</legend>
<label class="practice-choice"><input type="radio" name="practice-group-09" value="A"><span><b>A.</b> It guarantees the vegetation causes any observed difference in erosion.</span></label>
<label class="practice-choice"><input type="radio" name="practice-group-09" value="B"><span><b>B.</b> It captures variation among streams instead of treating one stream segment as the whole watershed.</span></label>
<label class="practice-choice"><input type="radio" name="practice-group-09" value="C"><span><b>C.</b> It removes the need to measure erosion.</span></label>
<label class="practice-choice"><input type="radio" name="practice-group-09" value="D"><span><b>D.</b> It makes within-stream spatial correlation impossible.</span></label>
</fieldset>
</div>
<div class="practice-actions"><button type="button" class="practice-reveal" disabled aria-controls="practice-solution-09" aria-expanded="false">Show explained answer</button><span class="practice-status" aria-live="polite"></span></div>

::: {.practice-solution #practice-solution-09 hidden="hidden"}

**Suggested answer and reasoning**

1. **Read the scale in the question.** The researcher wants to understand the vegetation–erosion relationship *across a watershed*. That is broader than describing erosion along one short stream reach.
2. **See what twelve nearby plots can tell you.** They may show variation along that particular stream. But they share its rainfall, geology, land use and flow regime. Those plots are not twelve separate examples of how streams vary across the watershed.
3. **Why is B preferable?** Three plots on each of four streams give information from four stream systems instead of one. The plots still describe variation *within* streams, while differences *among* streams become observable.
4. **What could still complicate the comparison?** If streams with more vegetation also have gentler banks, you cannot assume the vegetation caused lower erosion. Record bank gradient, stream size, discharge or other conditions relevant to the question. Four streams may also be too few for some broad conclusions.
5. **When might the first design be useful?** If your question is about fine-scale changes in erosion along one specified reach, closely spaced plots might be appropriate.

Option **B** gives a better spatial starting point for the stated watershed question. Sampling more widely improves **coverage of among-stream variation**; it does not automatically prove causation or eliminate spatial dependence within streams.

:::

:::


::: {.practice-exercise #practice-10 data-mode="matching"}

<span class="practice-number">Exercise 10</span>

**What does the time question require?**

The same landscape can generate several different questions about time. Match each to the most informative starting design.

**Your task.** Choose the primary temporal strategy for each question.

<div class="practice-response" data-mode="matching">
<div class="practice-matches"><p class="practice-label">Choose one design or interpretation for each statement.</p>
<label class="practice-match"><span class="practice-match-statement">What fraction of marked seedlings survives during the next three years?</span><select aria-label="Match for item 1 in exercise 10" data-answer="B"><option value="">Choose…</option>
<option value="A">A. Repeat measurements around rain events, including a pre-event baseline when feasible.</option>
<option value="B">B. Follow identified individuals at successive censuses.</option>
<option value="C">C. Sample across both day types, at comparable times, over representative weeks.</option>
<option value="D">D. Use before-and-after monitoring in intervention and comparison streams.</option>
</select></label>
<label class="practice-match"><span class="practice-match-statement">How does park use vary between weekdays and weekends?</span><select aria-label="Match for item 2 in exercise 10" data-answer="C"><option value="">Choose…</option>
<option value="A">A. Repeat measurements around rain events, including a pre-event baseline when feasible.</option>
<option value="B">B. Follow identified individuals at successive censuses.</option>
<option value="C">C. Sample across both day types, at comparable times, over representative weeks.</option>
<option value="D">D. Use before-and-after monitoring in intervention and comparison streams.</option>
</select></label>
<label class="practice-match"><span class="practice-match-statement">Did water turbidity change after a restoration intervention compared with similar untreated streams?</span><select aria-label="Match for item 3 in exercise 10" data-answer="D"><option value="">Choose…</option>
<option value="A">A. Repeat measurements around rain events, including a pre-event baseline when feasible.</option>
<option value="B">B. Follow identified individuals at successive censuses.</option>
<option value="C">C. Sample across both day types, at comparable times, over representative weeks.</option>
<option value="D">D. Use before-and-after monitoring in intervention and comparison streams.</option>
</select></label>
<label class="practice-match"><span class="practice-match-statement">What is the short-term turbidity response to heavy rain?</span><select aria-label="Match for item 4 in exercise 10" data-answer="A"><option value="">Choose…</option>
<option value="A">A. Repeat measurements around rain events, including a pre-event baseline when feasible.</option>
<option value="B">B. Follow identified individuals at successive censuses.</option>
<option value="C">C. Sample across both day types, at comparable times, over representative weeks.</option>
<option value="D">D. Use before-and-after monitoring in intervention and comparison streams.</option>
</select></label>
</div>
</div>
<div class="practice-actions"><button type="button" class="practice-reveal" disabled aria-controls="practice-solution-10" aria-expanded="false">Show explained answer</button><span class="practice-status" aria-live="polite"></span></div>

::: {.practice-solution #practice-solution-10 hidden="hidden"}

**Suggested answer and reasoning**

1. **Marked seedling survival — B.** To learn what fraction survive over three years, you need to find the **same seedlings** again. A new set of seedlings every year could describe abundance but not the fate of the original group.
2. **Weekdays versus weekends — C.** Observe both kinds of day, at comparable times. Otherwise a difference between a Saturday afternoon and a Monday morning could reflect time of day rather than the weekday–weekend contrast.
3. **Intervention effect on turbidity — D.** Measure treated streams and comparable untreated streams before and after the intervention. That way you can see whether change in treated streams differs from change happening more generally. Rainfall and discharge still need consideration.
4. **Short-term response to rain — A.** Turbidity may rise and fall over hours. Measurements once a month, or even once a week, could miss the event. Sample around rain events, including before and during or shortly after them when feasible.
5. **Match the observation frequency to the process.** A three-year study can contain very different schedules: annual plant censuses, repeated visitor counts during selected days, and rapid measurements during storms. Duration alone does not tell you whether your sampling can capture the process.

Each strategy follows from *the time scale of the question and the comparison needed*. There is no universally appropriate measurement interval.

:::

:::


::: {.practice-exercise #practice-11 data-mode="text"}

<span class="practice-number">Exercise 11</span>

**What would monthly river sampling miss?**

A team proposes to sample stream turbidity on the first Monday of every month for three years. Its main question is whether restoration reduces sediment pulses during heavy storms.

**Your task.** Explain one change to the sampling schedule and one comparison needed to assess the proposed effect.

<div class="practice-response" data-mode="text">
<label class="practice-label" for="practice-input-11">Your answer</label>
<textarea id="practice-input-11" class="practice-text" rows="3" placeholder="Write a brief answer. Explain your sampling decision and why it fits the question."></textarea>
</div>
<div class="practice-actions"><button type="button" class="practice-reveal" disabled aria-controls="practice-solution-11" aria-expanded="false">Show explained answer</button><span class="practice-status" aria-live="polite"></span></div>

::: {.practice-solution #practice-solution-11 hidden="hidden"}

**Suggested answer and reasoning**

1. **Begin with what a sediment pulse is.** After a heavy storm, suspended sediment and turbidity can rise rapidly and then fall. A water sample taken on the first Monday of each month may miss nearly all of those short peaks.
2. **Change the schedule to match the events.** Record rainfall and stream discharge and collect turbidity observations at short intervals during a set of storms. An automated sensor may help, but an appropriately planned event-sampling schedule could also be used. It is useful to know conditions before the rain and during the rise and fall of the storm response.
3. **Ask what would have happened without restoration.** Even if turbidity peaks decline after planting, storms may have been smaller in later years. To assess an intervention effect, include comparable untreated streams, or another carefully justified reference, measured during the same period.
4. **Make comparisons meaningful.** Compare similar storm conditions where possible, and account for differences in rainfall intensity, discharge and seasonal context. Turbidity is also an indicator of suspended particles, not a direct measurement of the total mass of eroded soil.
5. **State the conclusion carefully.** With event observations you can describe sediment-related responses to storms. With appropriate treated–untreated and before–after comparisons, you can investigate whether those responses changed differently after restoration. Without these comparisons, you cannot confidently attribute the change to restoration.

A useful answer names **one event-focused sampling change** and **one comparison**. The essential lesson is that a monthly schedule may be long enough in calendar time but too sparse to observe the process of interest.

:::

:::


::: {.practice-exercise #practice-12 data-mode="single"}

<span class="practice-number">Exercise 12</span>

**Detectability is part of the sampling design**

Bird counts are conducted once in dense regenerating forest and once in adjacent open grassland. The researcher concludes that the forest has fewer bird species because fewer were detected there during the surveys.

**Your task.** Which change most directly addresses a weakness in that conclusion?

<div class="practice-response" data-mode="single">
<fieldset class="practice-choices" data-correct="A"><legend>Select the best answer</legend>
<label class="practice-choice"><input type="radio" name="practice-group-12" value="A"><span><b>A.</b> Repeat standardised surveys across sites and conditions, recording factors affecting detection, and choose an approach that accounts for imperfect detection where appropriate.</span></label>
<label class="practice-choice"><input type="radio" name="practice-group-12" value="B"><span><b>B.</b> Use a longer species list from the open grassland.</span></label>
<label class="practice-choice"><input type="radio" name="practice-group-12" value="C"><span><b>C.</b> Count only the loudest birds because they are easiest to identify.</span></label>
</fieldset>
</div>
<div class="practice-actions"><button type="button" class="practice-reveal" disabled aria-controls="practice-solution-12" aria-expanded="false">Show explained answer</button><span class="practice-status" aria-live="polite"></span></div>

::: {.practice-solution #practice-solution-12 hidden="hidden"}

**Suggested answer and reasoning**

1. **Distinguish the birds from what the observer notices.** A bird species may be present in a forest but unseen or unheard during a particular visit. Dense vegetation, weather, species behaviour, observer skill and time of day affect what is detected.
2. **Interpret the existing data correctly.** The observations show that **fewer species were detected** in the forest during those visits. They do *not* yet establish that fewer species were present there.
3. **Why choose A?** Repeated surveys, carried out using comparable effort and conditions at several sites in each habitat, help describe how detections vary. Recording distance, visibility, listening conditions or other relevant factors can help evaluate differences in detection probability.
4. **Keep replication and detection distinct.** Revisiting one forest site many times helps with the observation problem at that site. Sampling multiple forest sites helps you learn about forests more broadly. A sound design may need both.
5. **What can the improved study conclude?** Depending on the sampling method and analysis, the observations may support comparisons of occupancy, occurrence or abundance while allowing for imperfect detection. Simply counting louder birds, or adding species to only one habitat's list, would not solve the bias.

The starting question should be: *Could the observed difference be due partly to how easily animals were detected?* If so, the sampling design must address that possibility.

:::

:::


## C. Evaluate and improve a research design

These situations ask you to diagnose what the proposed observations would establish, which alternative explanations they leave open, and what changes would strengthen the design.


::: {.practice-exercise #practice-13 data-mode="text"}

<span class="practice-number">Exercise 13</span>

**Who is missing from the interviews?**

A researcher wants to understand why residents avoid a new park route. They interview people walking along the route between 10 a.m. and 2 p.m. on two sunny weekdays.

**Your task.** Identify two gaps in the participant sample and propose a feasible recruitment change for each.

<div class="practice-response" data-mode="text">
<label class="practice-label" for="practice-input-13">Your answer</label>
<textarea id="practice-input-13" class="practice-text" rows="3" placeholder="Write a brief answer. Explain your sampling decision and why it fits the question."></textarea>
</div>
<div class="practice-actions"><button type="button" class="practice-reveal" disabled aria-controls="practice-solution-13" aria-expanded="false">Show explained answer</button><span class="practice-status" aria-live="polite"></span></div>

::: {.practice-solution #practice-solution-13 hidden="hidden"}

**Suggested answer and reasoning**

1. **Ask who could possibly be interviewed.** The team stands *on the path*. A resident who avoids the path entirely cannot be approached there. That is the first important gap—and it directly concerns the research question.
2. **Find those missing non-users.** Recruit through nearby residential areas, community groups, other park entrances or routes. Ask about their destinations and route choices, including people who rarely visit the park at all.
3. **Look at when interviews occurred.** Two sunny weekdays between 10 a.m. and 2 p.m. exclude many people who work at those times and people who visit during evenings or weekends. Their concerns might differ from those of daytime visitors.
4. **Add contrasting occasions.** Recruit on some evenings and weekends and, if relevant, under different conditions. Explain why you expect these occasions to bring in different types of experience, rather than simply increasing the number of interviews.
5. **Connect the sample back to the claim.** Interviews with daytime path users can tell you what those people experience. They cannot, by themselves, explain why *residents who do not use the path* avoid it. A purposeful sample that includes different relevant groups is more informative for this question.

Two good answers would name **non-users** and **people absent at the selected interview times**, then give a feasible way to reach each group. There are other reasonable answers if the missing perspectives and proposed recruitment are justified.

:::

:::


::: {.practice-exercise #practice-14 data-mode="single"}

<span class="practice-number">Exercise 14</span>

**Can a before–after difference show an effect?**

One stream receives an erosion-control intervention. Turbidity is measured for one wet season before and one after. Post-intervention values are lower, but rainfall was also lower in the second season.

**Your task.** Which modification would most strengthen an investigation of the intervention effect?

<div class="practice-response" data-mode="single">
<fieldset class="practice-choices" data-correct="B"><legend>Select the best answer</legend>
<label class="practice-choice"><input type="radio" name="practice-group-14" value="A"><span><b>A.</b> Measure turbidity more frequently after the intervention but not before.</span></label>
<label class="practice-choice"><input type="radio" name="practice-group-14" value="B"><span><b>B.</b> Add suitable untreated comparison streams with before-and-after measurements, alongside rainfall and discharge observations.</span></label>
<label class="practice-choice"><input type="radio" name="practice-group-14" value="C"><span><b>C.</b> Ignore rainfall because the same stream was measured twice.</span></label>
</fieldset>
</div>
<div class="practice-actions"><button type="button" class="practice-reveal" disabled aria-controls="practice-solution-14" aria-expanded="false">Show explained answer</button><span class="practice-status" aria-live="polite"></span></div>

::: {.practice-solution #practice-solution-14 hidden="hidden"}

**Suggested answer and reasoning**

1. **Begin with the observed change.** Turbidity was lower after the intervention. That is a real before–after difference in the available records.
2. **Find another possible cause.** Rainfall was also lower. Less rain can mean less runoff and sediment transport, even if the erosion-control intervention has no effect. The study cannot yet separate these explanations.
3. **Choose B: compare changes across streams.** Monitor several appropriate untreated streams as well as treated ones, before and after the intervention. Ask whether turbidity changed **more** in the treated streams than in the comparisons, under comparable rainfall and flow conditions.
4. **See why more measurements *after* treatment are insufficient.** Option A provides a better description of the later period, but does not supply the missing comparison with what might have happened without treatment. Option C ignores an obvious alternative explanation.
5. **Recognise the remaining limitation.** Untreated streams are not perfect copies of the treated ones. They could differ in land use, channel shape, upstream disturbance or hydrology. Measuring these differences and selecting comparisons carefully improves the study; random assignment of interventions, when feasible, would strengthen causal inference further.

A good causal comparison tries to estimate what change would have occurred *without the intervention*. A simple before–after record from one stream usually cannot do that.

:::

:::


::: {.practice-exercise #practice-15 data-mode="multi"}

<span class="practice-number">Exercise 15</span>

**Which measurements support a carbon-stock estimate?**

A team wants to estimate soil organic carbon stock down to a defined soil depth across a restored mangrove. It has satellite imagery of vegetation greenness, measurements of soil organic carbon concentration and dry bulk density from cores reaching the specified depth, and a map of the mangrove area.

**Your task.** Which statements follow from these measurements and a suitably designed spatial sample? Select all that apply.

<div class="practice-response" data-mode="multi">
<fieldset class="practice-choices"><legend>Select all the statements you think are supported</legend>
<label class="practice-choice"><input type="checkbox" value="A" data-answer="true"><span><b>A.</b> Carbon concentration, bulk density and depth can be combined to estimate soil carbon stock for sampled soil layers.</span></label>
<label class="practice-choice"><input type="checkbox" value="B" data-answer="false"><span><b>B.</b> Satellite greenness alone directly measures soil organic carbon stock throughout the landscape.</span></label>
<label class="practice-choice"><input type="checkbox" value="C" data-answer="true"><span><b>C.</b> An island-wide estimate also requires a justified way to represent or model spatial variation between sampled locations.</span></label>
<label class="practice-choice"><input type="checkbox" value="D" data-answer="false"><span><b>D.</b> Measuring many cores at a single convenient site guarantees a representative landscape estimate.</span></label>
</fieldset>
</div>
<div class="practice-actions"><button type="button" class="practice-reveal" disabled aria-controls="practice-solution-15" aria-expanded="false">Show explained answer</button><span class="practice-status" aria-live="polite"></span></div>

::: {.practice-solution #practice-solution-15 hidden="hidden"}

**Suggested answer and reasoning**

1. **Identify what a stock means.** Soil carbon *concentration* tells you what proportion of the sampled dry soil mass is carbon. A **stock** asks how much carbon is stored beneath a specified area, down to a specified depth.
2. **Work out the calculation in words.** Bulk density tells you how much dry soil mass there is per unit volume. Multiplying soil volume (area × depth) by bulk density gives soil mass. Multiplying that mass by the measured carbon fraction gives carbon mass. This is why **A** is supported, assuming the sampled depth, units and soil material are handled consistently.
3. **Distinguish the point estimate from the landscape estimate.** A core estimates the stock at its sampled location. To estimate the entire mangrove, you must decide how sampled locations represent different sediment conditions across the area—for example through a spatial sampling design or an appropriately justified model. That makes **C** correct.
4. **Why B is wrong.** Satellite greenness records a property of vegetation. It does not directly measure carbon stored below ground. It might help build a model with field data, but such a model would have assumptions and uncertainty.
5. **Why D is wrong.** Forty cores at one convenient site may give a good estimate of that site's soil, but tell you little about other mangrove areas if sediment conditions vary.

Choose **A and C**. Always ask two separate questions: *How is the quantity calculated at a sampled point?* and *How will the sampled points represent the larger area?*

:::

:::


::: {.practice-exercise #practice-16 data-mode="text"}

<span class="practice-number">Exercise 16</span>

**What can the observations establish?**

A chronosequence of naturally regenerating forest sites shows higher tree richness in older sites. The older forests are also closer to remnant mature forest and have had less intensive previous land use.

**Your task.** State a conclusion supported by the observations and propose one additional comparison or measurement that would help distinguish age from the other explanations.

<div class="practice-response" data-mode="text">
<label class="practice-label" for="practice-input-16">Your answer</label>
<textarea id="practice-input-16" class="practice-text" rows="3" placeholder="Write a brief answer. Explain your sampling decision and why it fits the question."></textarea>
</div>
<div class="practice-actions"><button type="button" class="practice-reveal" disabled aria-controls="practice-solution-16" aria-expanded="false">Show explained answer</button><span class="practice-status" aria-live="polite"></span></div>

::: {.practice-solution #practice-solution-16 hidden="hidden"}

**Suggested answer and reasoning**

1. **State only what was observed.** Older forest sites in this particular sample have more tree species than younger sites, under the sampling method used. That is a pattern *across different sites*.
2. **Ask whether those sites differ in other relevant ways.** The older sites are also closer to mature forest and have experienced less intensive land use. Nearby forest may supply more seeds, while past land use may affect soils or surviving vegetation. Either could help explain the richness difference.
3. **Understand the problem with calling it succession.** The study did not observe these younger forests becoming older. It compared forests of different present ages. It therefore cannot tell, from this pattern alone, how much richness would increase as *one given forest* ages.
4. **Improve the comparison.** One option is to add younger and older sites at similar distances from mature forest and with similar land-use histories. Another is to return repeatedly to the same sites and measure richness change through time. Both approaches help, but in different ways.
5. **Consider what you actually count.** Species richness can also depend on plot area and the number of stems examined. Use comparable sampling effort across sites and be clear whether your question concerns richness per unit area or richness at a given number of individuals.

A supported conclusion is: *In the sampled forests, older sites had higher observed tree richness.* A stronger conclusion that **age caused** the difference needs a design that examines alternative explanations.

:::

:::


## D. A connected restoration-study challenge

The final four exercises develop one study through successive decisions. Each answer informs the next choice. The aim is to see how question, sampling structure, observations and field effort fit together.


::: {.practice-exercise #practice-17 data-mode="text"}

<span class="practice-number">Decision 1</span>

**Challenge, decision 1: formulate the comparison**

**A connected design challenge.** A hypothetical restoration landscape contains six separately managed restoration blocks: three planted and three naturally regenerating. Each block has upper and lower slopes. Management approaches were chosen by landowners rather than assigned randomly, and earlier land use is not identical among blocks. The proposal covers three years and has a total fieldwork allowance of **720 person-hours**. Your aim is to investigate establishment of native woody seedlings.

**Your task.** Write one answerable research question. Identify its *main* response variable, the independent units for comparing restoration approaches, and one alternative explanation for a difference you might observe.

<div class="practice-response" data-mode="text">
<label class="practice-label" for="practice-input-17">Your answer</label>
<textarea id="practice-input-17" class="practice-text" rows="3" placeholder="Write a brief answer. Explain your sampling decision and why it fits the question."></textarea>
</div>
<div class="practice-actions"><button type="button" class="practice-reveal" disabled aria-controls="practice-solution-17" aria-expanded="false">Show explained answer</button><span class="practice-status" aria-live="polite"></span></div>

::: {.practice-solution #practice-solution-17 hidden="hidden"}

**Suggested answer and reasoning**

1. **Choose a question that the available study can actually investigate.** One option is: *How does the number of new native woody seedlings recorded per plot between annual censuses differ among planted and naturally regenerating blocks, and between upper and lower slopes?*
2. **Name a primary response.** For this question, use the **number of newly recorded live native seedlings per fixed plot area over each census interval**, or convert it to a comparable rate. This is more informative than a one-time count of all seedlings. With annual censuses, it counts seedlings that are alive and detectable when the next census occurs; seedlings that emerged and died between visits will be missed. Survival of marked seedlings could be a useful *additional* response, but it is a separate quantity.
3. **Find the correct unit for comparing approaches.** There are six separately managed **blocks**, three per approach. These are the main site-level units of the restoration comparison. Plots are selected *within* the blocks; individual seedlings are observed within plots.
4. **Identify a credible alternative explanation.** If planted blocks previously had less intensive farming, they might have better soil or more surviving seed sources. That difference could affect recruitment even without an effect of planting. Record land-use history or other relevant baseline conditions.
5. **Set the strength of the conclusion.** Management was chosen by landowners, not randomly assigned. The study can compare recruitment patterns associated with the two approaches, but attributing any difference solely to planting would require stronger control of initial differences.

Many research questions are possible. A useful answer should make clear **what varies, what you will measure, which units you compare, and what else could explain the pattern**.

:::

:::


::: {.practice-exercise #practice-18 data-mode="single"}

<span class="practice-number">Decision 2</span>

**Challenge, decision 2: distribute the plots**

**A connected design challenge.** A hypothetical restoration landscape contains six separately managed restoration blocks: three planted and three naturally regenerating. Each block has upper and lower slopes. Management approaches were chosen by landowners rather than assigned randomly, and earlier land use is not identical among blocks. The proposal covers three years and has a total fieldwork allowance of **720 person-hours**. Your aim is to investigate establishment of native woody seedlings.

**Your task.** Which strategy gives the most useful spatial structure while retaining the existing six blocks?

<div class="practice-response" data-mode="single">
<fieldset class="practice-choices" data-correct="B"><legend>Select the best answer</legend>
<label class="practice-choice"><input type="radio" name="practice-group-18" value="A"><span><b>A.</b> Locate all 24 plots in the most accessible planted block.</span></label>
<label class="practice-choice"><input type="radio" name="practice-group-18" value="B"><span><b>B.</b> In each block, randomly choose two eligible plot locations on upper slopes and two on lower slopes, producing 24 plots in total.</span></label>
<label class="practice-choice"><input type="radio" name="practice-group-18" value="C"><span><b>C.</b> Place twelve plots in one planted block and twelve in one naturally regenerating block, treating all plots as independent treatment replicates.</span></label>
</fieldset>
</div>
<div class="practice-actions"><button type="button" class="practice-reveal" disabled aria-controls="practice-solution-18" aria-expanded="false">Show explained answer</button><span class="practice-status" aria-live="polite"></span></div>

::: {.practice-solution #practice-solution-18 hidden="hidden"}

**Suggested answer and reasoning**

1. **Write out the comparisons.** The study has two management approaches, with three independently managed blocks under each. Within every block are upper and lower slopes. The design should include both slope positions and all six blocks.
2. **Choose B and count the plots.** Two plots on the upper slope plus two on the lower slope gives **four plots per block**. Across six blocks, that gives **6 × 4 = 24 plots**.
3. **Why select within slope groups?** If plots were placed without regard to slope, one block might have mostly upper-slope plots while another had mostly lower-slope plots. Sampling both positions in every block makes those conditions comparable across the blocks.
4. **Where does random selection fit?** First define eligible upper- and lower-slope areas. Then draw the designated plot locations within each area randomly. Random selection helps avoid choosing only convenient or especially healthy-looking patches; it does not replace the earlier decision to sample both slope positions.
5. **Keep the units straight.** There are 24 plots, but still only **six independently managed blocks**, three per approach. The plots help describe variation within a block. They do not create 24 independent replicates of the management approach.

Option A would concentrate observations in one planted block. Option C would compare just one block per approach. Both would lose important site-level coverage. Because management was not assigned randomly, even option B provides an *observational comparison*, not a controlled treatment experiment.

:::

:::


::: {.practice-exercise #practice-19 data-mode="matching"}

<span class="practice-number">Decision 3</span>

**Challenge, decision 3: what and when to measure?**

**A connected design challenge.** A hypothetical restoration landscape contains six separately managed restoration blocks: three planted and three naturally regenerating. Each block has upper and lower slopes. Management approaches were chosen by landowners rather than assigned randomly, and earlier land use is not identical among blocks. The proposal covers three years and has a total fieldwork allowance of **720 person-hours**. Your aim is to investigate establishment of native woody seedlings.

**Your task.** To compare newly recorded seedlings and the survival of marked seedlings, while considering alternative explanations, match each information need to an observation.

<div class="practice-response" data-mode="matching">

</select></label>

<option value="A">A. Map proximity to remnant forest and, if feasible, measure seed arrival at appropriately distributed locations.</option>
<option value="B">B. Record baseline management history, land use, slope and relevant soil conditions for each block.</option>
<option value="C">C. Revisit permanent plots at comparable intervals and identify seedlings not recorded at the previous census.</option>
<option value="D">D. Tag or map individuals and check their status at successive visits.</option>
</select></label>
</div>
</div>
<div class="practice-actions"><button type="button" class="practice-reveal" disabled aria-controls="practice-solution-19" aria-expanded="false">Show explained answer</button><span class="practice-status" aria-live="polite"></span></div>

::: {.practice-solution #practice-solution-19 hidden="hidden"}

**Suggested answer and reasoning**

1. **Newly recorded live seedlings — C.** Revisit the same permanent plots, record each live seedling, and identify which individuals were *not present in the previous census*. These are new individuals recorded at the later visit. Using the same plot area and census rules lets you compare rates among blocks.
2. **Survival — D.** Mark or map individual seedlings, then check whether each is alive at the next visit. If you simply count the total number each year, a dead seedling replaced by a new one could leave the total unchanged; you would miss the death.
3. **Initial conditions — B.** Record slope position, soils, earlier land use and management history. Otherwise observed recruitment differences between approaches might reflect pre-existing environmental or historical differences.
4. **Seed availability — A.** Note the distance to mature forest and, if relevant and feasible, measure seed arrival. Distance is a *possible indicator* of seed supply; it does not directly measure how many viable seeds arrive at a particular plot.
5. **Recognise the census interval limitation.** A seedling might appear after one annual visit and die before the next. Annual censuses will never record it. The study therefore estimates **new seedlings surviving until the next census**, not every germination or establishment event that occurred during the year. If short-term emergence and early mortality are central to the question, visit more frequently.

These observations answer different parts of the investigation. They are complementary, but one does not automatically substitute for the others.

:::

:::


::: {.practice-exercise #practice-20 data-mode="single"}

<span class="practice-number">Decision 4</span>

**Challenge, decision 4: stay within 720 hours**

**A connected design challenge.** A hypothetical restoration landscape contains six separately managed restoration blocks: three planted and three naturally regenerating. Each block has upper and lower slopes. Management approaches were chosen by landowners rather than assigned randomly, and earlier land use is not identical among blocks. The proposal covers three years and has a total fieldwork allowance of **720 person-hours**. Your aim is to investigate establishment of native woody seedlings.

Assume a field census requires **3 person-hours per permanent plot**, and that you will undertake four censuses (baseline and the ends of three years). Travel between blocks requires **120 person-hours** over the whole project; setup and training **80 hours**; and identification and data checks **70 hours**. Compare two within-block sampling plans:

- **Plan X:** three plots per slope position in every block (36 plots).
- **Plan Y:** two plots per slope position in every block (24 plots).

**Your task.** Which plan would leave a more credible reserve for weather, failed visits and follow-up checks?

<div class="practice-response" data-mode="single">
<fieldset class="practice-choices" data-correct="B"><legend>Select the best answer</legend>
<label class="practice-choice"><input type="radio" name="practice-group-20" value="A"><span><b>A.</b> Plan X. It uses 702 hours and leaves 18 hours.</span></label>
<label class="practice-choice"><input type="radio" name="practice-group-20" value="B"><span><b>B.</b> Plan Y. It uses 558 hours and leaves 162 hours.</span></label>
<label class="practice-choice"><input type="radio" name="practice-group-20" value="C"><span><b>C.</b> Both use exactly 720 hours.</span></label>
<label class="practice-choice"><input type="radio" name="practice-group-20" value="D"><span><b>D.</b> The number of plots does not affect fieldwork hours.</span></label>
</fieldset>
</div>
<div class="practice-actions"><button type="button" class="practice-reveal" disabled aria-controls="practice-solution-20" aria-expanded="false">Show explained answer</button><span class="practice-status" aria-live="polite"></span></div>

::: {.practice-solution #practice-solution-20 hidden="hidden"}

**Suggested answer and reasoning**

1. **Calculate census effort.** Plan X has 36 plots, measured four times, at 3 person-hours each: **36 × 4 × 3 = 432 person-hours**. Plan Y needs **24 × 4 × 3 = 288 person-hours**.
2. **Add the fixed project costs.** Travel is 120 hours, setup and training 80, and identification and data checks 70. Together that is **270 person-hours** for either plan.
3. **Compare each total with the 720-hour allowance.** Plan X uses **432 + 270 = 702 hours**, leaving **720 − 702 = 18 hours**. Plan Y uses **288 + 270 = 558 hours**, leaving **720 − 558 = 162 hours**. The correct answer is **B**.
4. **Think beyond the calculation.** Eighteen person-hours across a three-year field study leave little scope for rain delays, missed plots, replacements or necessary repeat visits. Plan Y retains the same six blocks and both slope positions, but with fewer plots per position, and leaves a much more useful reserve.
5. **Understand the trade-off.** Fewer plots may make the estimate for each block less precise. However, both plans still have only three blocks per management approach. Adding plots within blocks does not add independent management replicates.
6. **Use contingencies as part of the design.** Keep some hours unallocated for problems likely to arise. If you later add measurements, choose those that directly improve the answer to your research question, not simply those that are interesting to collect.

The arithmetic assumes the stated costs are correct and that one census of every plot takes the same average effort. Real proposals would need to justify those assumptions too. The best plan is the one that answers the question with realistic effort, not automatically the plan with the most plots.

:::

:::


## What to take into your assessment

A good sampling proposal connects the research question to a target population, independent units, appropriate comparisons, meaningful coverage across space and time, and the field effort available. You should also be able to explain what your observations would establish and which relationships remain partly inferred. A clear justification for a focused, feasible design is more useful than a long inventory of techniques.
